lines.text: Well a pleasant October evening to you, wherever you happen to be tuned in tonight. Welcome along to American Family Field for the start of the World Series. Tampa Bay and Milwaukee, zero and zero in the fall classic, and the air is just crisp enough to remind you why we play this game deep into the autumn. Nick Martinez is on the hill for the Rays, and Jacob Misiorowski gets the ball for our Brewers. Let us settle right in.

Well the man standing in first for Tampa Bay will be looking at thirty-six year old Nick Martinez, the Miami born right-hander they call Tricky who made his big-league debut way back in twenty-four. At six-foot-one, he has been around the block a time or two. Up against him is our tall young fellow Jacob Misiorowski, all six-foot-seven of him from Blue Springs, Missouri, making his first fall classic appearance after breaking into the bigs just this year at age twenty-four.
Yandy Díaz comes up, first pitch, four-seam fastball at 104, soft one, right in the zone. Count’s now one ball, zero strikes. Aranita’s got a steady eye, just like he’s done all season.
with the count 1 and 0: Four-Seam Fastball 102 mph, swinging strike, making the count 1 and 1
Jacob Misiorowski’s got the first pitch, count's 1-1, no one on base, just trying to keep the inning clean — and Aranita Diaz, with that .308 clip, ready to turn it around.

Misiorowski fires another hundred-mile-an-hour fastball, Díaz lifts it out toward right field, Sal Frelick drifts back and hauls it in easily for the first out, still no score here in the top of the first.
Christian Yelich hit for the cycle twice against the Reds in twenty eighteen.
Count’s 0 and 1. Aranda takes the first pitch, a four-seam fastball at 103, right in the zone. He’s got a steady hand, like he’s done all season, with that .257 clip in the postseason.
Misiorowski comes right back with another four-seam fastball, one hundred three miles an hour, and Aranda tips it foul, keeping us at zero and two here in the top of the first.
Aranda’s got that 6-foot frame, built for the big leagues, and he’s been hitting .257 in the postseason—steady stuff, like he’s found his rhythm already.

Right into right field for a base hit off the bat of Jonathan Aranda at ninety miles an hour, dropping safely in front of Sal Frelick for a single, and the Rays have a runner on first with one out here in the top of the first, still no score.
Reminds me of my single summer in Class D, where my glove had more holes than a piece of Swiss cheese. Misiorowski checks the runner at first.

Four-seam fastball, 102, ball, count now 1 and 0. Simpson, 25, just stepped in from Atlanta, fresh in the big leagues, looking sharp. One out, runner on first, still no score, Misiorowski keeping the plate tight.
Foul ball on a four-seam, 101, count now 1 and 1. Simpson, fresh from Atlanta, looks sharp, but Misiorowski keeps the plate tight. One out, runners on first, still no score.
Still no runs on the board, just one out and a runner on first, Brewers and Rays both holding steady at zero, like the night hasn't even started yet.

Runners on first, one out, count now 1 and 2. Four-seam fastball, 101, swinging strike. Simpson, fresh from Atlanta, stays in the zone, Misiorowski keeps the plate tight. Still no runs, no lead, just tension building in the top of the first.
Misiorowski’s on the mound, tall and steady, watching the corners of the infield—Simpson’s got range in center, but the gap in left’s open, and the shift’s gotta be tight.
Simpson swings at a four-seam fastball, 103, foul. Count stays 1 and 2. One out, runners on first, still no score. Misiorowski keeps the plate tight, Simpson staying in the zone.
Misiorowski’s got six pitches in the books, steady through the first, no walks, no runs — just a solid start in the opening frame, keeping the plate tight like he’s been doing since his debut.

Misiorowski deals the eighty-eight mile per hour curveball, Simpson grounds it softly to left fielder Jackson Chourio for a single, Jonathan Aranda jogs over to second, runners now on first and second, still no score in the top of the first.
Runners on first and second, one out, no strikes, no balls — Simpson’s got a chance to set the tone, Misiorowski’s got to keep the infield clean. First pitch of the inning, and it’s all on the line.

Junior Caminero steps up, count at zero, zero. Misiorowski fires a four-seam fastball, 102, soft in the zone, a ball. The count now stands at one ball, zero strikes. First pitch of the inning, no pressure yet, just the wind in the field.

Misiorowski ahead in the count now, twenty-three year old Junior Caminero from Santo Domingo facing that ninety-six mile per hour cutter. He hits it softly, just a seventy-six mile per hour line drive out toward third baseman David Hamilton who fires to Brice Turang to complete the double play Hamilton to Turang, they turn it with a thing of beauty, two quick ones right there to erase the trouble and we are still scoreless after half an inning

Top of the first in the books, no runs on two hits for Tampa Bay, and we are still scoreless. Prince Fielder gave us fifty home runs back in two thousand seven, folks. Let's see what our boys can do against the righty when we come right back.
A quick tip of the cap to the wizard behind the curtain, Josh Stutting. He built this whole booth out of ones and zeros. For your technology and wizardry needs, stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
Twenty-three year old Junior Caminero stepping back in, born down in Santo Domingo, carrying that postseason average of two hundred seventy-three into the box.

Nick Martinez looks in, no balls and no strikes to the twenty-two year old Jackson Chourio born down in Maracaibo, Venezuela, and he deals a ninety-one mile per hour cutter Chourio swings and he laces it, a line drive out to right field and he's got himself a single to get us started right here in the bottom of the first!
Pickoff attempt at first base, short and sharp, just barely missed — that’s how the pitcher keeps the game tight. Jake Bauers comes up, count at zero, zero. The night’s just beginning.

Nick Martinez starts with a 91 mile per hour cutter, ball, count now one and zero. Jake Bauers takes it easy, just a little pause there, and the count settles in. First base holds firm, still nobody out.

Sinker at 95, called strike, count now one and one. Jake Bauers stays steady, just a touch of hesitation there. First base still holding, no one's gone yet. The pitcher keeps it tight with a clean delivery.

Nick Martinez fires a slider, 86 miles per hour, called strike, count now 1 and 2. Jake Bauers, 31, from Newport Beach, takes it slow, just a flick of the wrist, first base still holding. The count hangs there, waiting.

First pitch of the series, no one's scored yet, just a quiet start. Jake Bauers, 31, with a .269 average this post-season, steps up with one ball and two strikes. The game's just begun, and we're learning how it moves.
Martinez comes back with a cutter at ninety-two miles per hour, misses high. The count moves to two and two.

Jake Bauers walks in, 31, from Newport Beach, with a .269 clip this post-season—steady as a rock, just like the way he’s been since ’18. Tricky Martinez’s got the ball, but the night’s just getting warmed up.

Nick Martinez comes right back with a four-seam fastball at ninety-five miles per hour, fouled straight back. The count stays right where it was, two and two, with nobody out in the bottom of the first.
In twenty eighteen the Brewers came within one game of the World Series, losing Game Seven of the playoffs to the Dodgers.

Out to right field goes the changeup, seventy-nine miles per hour, tracked down and caught by Victor Mesa Junior. Bauers is retired on the fly ball, one away now in the bottom of the first, score still tied at zero.
No runs yet, just a quiet first inning, like the Brewers settling in before they ever really warm up. One out, runners on first, and the night's still just beginning.

Slider at 86, called strike. Count's now 0 and 1. Yelich sets his stance, eyes locked on Martinez. First pitch, no pressure yet, just a step toward the plate. One strike, one out away, the night's just starting.
Fastball at 95, swinging strike, count jumps to 0 and 2. Yelich stays back, eyes locked, the big man in the box, steady as always. One strike, one out away, the night’s just starting.

Changeup at 78, fouled back to the pitcher. Count stays 0 and 2. Martinez winds up slow, gloves low, bat in hand, ready to go again. Yelich steps in, eyes fixed, the first pitch of the at-bat just passed. One strike, one out away.
One out, runners on first, count at 0-2, Yelich ready to work through the count, Martinez keeping it tight, both sides waiting for the next pitch to move things forward.

Sinker at 94, fouled back to Martinez. Count stays 0 and 2. Yelich keeps his feet, eyes fixed on the plate, the pitcher tight, both sides holding steady, one out, runners on first, score still dead even.
Yelich’s been around the league since '13, hit over a third of the time in this post-season, steady as a rock, steady as a man with a long memory and a big frame.

Martinez stays with the cutter, spinning it toward the plate as Yelich swings and lifts a sharp line drive out toward center field where DeLuca gives chase and watches it drop! It races all the way to the wall, Chourio comes around to score easily, and Yelich cruises into third with a triple to put Milwaukee on top by a run!

Martinez winds and delivers a cutter at ninety-one, Contreras steps in and drives it hard! He lines it past the shortstop into left field for a sharp single, Yelich races home with the run, and Milwaukee tacks on another to lead two to nothing!
Mound visit, nothing changed. Turang takes a breath, sets his eyes on the plate.
Sinker at 94, foul. Count now 0 and 1. Turang stays set, eyes on the plate, Martinez tight as ever. One out, runners on first, Brewers up by two, still waiting for the next pitch to shift things.
Slider at 85, fouled back once more. Count goes to zero and two. Turang stands firm, bat wagging just a bit, Martinez staying right on his work with two men on and our boys still ahead.
First pitch of the series, and the Brewers are already two up. Turang's got a chance to make it three, and Martinez's got a 3.00 ERA to deal with.
Fastball at 94, clean ball, count now 1 and 2. Turang stays ready, eyes fixed on the plate, Martinez keeping the rhythm. One out, runners on first, Brewers still two up.
Martinez uncorks a changeup at seventy-eight, Turang swings through it and down he goes for the second out, leaving two men stranded as our boys hold that two-to-zero lead.
The next guy up, rookie Brice Turang, just got his first taste of the majors—two outs, two runs up, and a chance to make this series his own.
Slider at 86, foul. Count now 0 and 1. Mitchell stays set, eyes on the plate, Martinez calm as always. Two outs, runners on first, Brewers up by two. Still waiting for the next pitch to shift things.

Martinez fires a changeup at 79, Mitchell swings and misses, count goes to zero and two. The fastball had a long arm, but the changeup cut through like a whisper. Mitchell stands tall, eyes locked on the plate. Two outs, runners on first, Brewers still two up.

Martinez comes right back with a four-seam fastball at ninety-four miles an hour, Mitchell fights it off into the screen for another foul ball, and our count stays steady at zero and two with two down and two men aboard here in the bottom of the first.

Changeup at 79, ball in dirt. Count now 1 and 2. Mitchell stays set, eyes on the plate. Two outs, runners on first, Brewers up by two. Martinez keeps the rhythm, hands steady, waiting for the next move.

Two outs, runners on first, Brewers up by two. Changeup at 79, ball in the dirt, count now 2 and 2. Mitchell stays set, eyes on the plate. Martinez keeps the rhythm, hands steady, waiting for the next move.
Sinker at 94, ball, count now 3 and 2. Mitchell stays set, eyes on the plate. Two outs, runners on first, Brewers up by two. Martinez keeps the rhythm, hands steady, waiting for the next pitch.

Back in my brief stint behind the plate in the minors, I once dropped three popups in a single inning while chasing a stray hot dog vendor. Martinez gets the sign from the catcher, checks the runner at first, and brings it home.

Full count now, three and three. Martinez delivers a changeup at seventy-seven miles an hour, Mitchell swings and misses, he is out. That ends the inning, three outs, bases empty, our score remains Brewers two, Rays zero.

And that brings us to the end of the first frame with the Brewers holding a two to zero lead on three hits to two. You know, folks, this franchise goes all the way back to nineteen sixty-nine as the Seattle Pilots before coming to Milwaukee the next year. Let us step aside for a moment.
I never could hit a curveball, but Josh Stutting has never met a tech problem he couldn't send to the bleachers. Reach him at stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
Juan Nieves threw the first no-hitter in Brewers history in nineteen eighty-seven.

Four-seam fastball, 99 mph, called strike. Count now 0 and 1. Hicks, 27, from Toronto, steps into the box with a quiet presence. First pitch, no pressure yet. The plate is open, and the count starts moving.

The cutter slices through the zone at 97 mph, pops foul, the count now 0 and 2. Hicks stays calm, just like he did in the first inning. Misiorowski keeps the rhythm, working the strike zone with precision. Bases stay empty, top of the second continues.

Misiorowski comes back with a cutter at ninety-six miles an hour, Hicks rolls it slowly to second, Turang picks it cleanly and throws to Bauers for the out, one away now in the second with the score still Brewers two, Rays zero.

Turang's in the hole at second, watching for any line drive down the middle, and Bauers at short is ready to roll if it heads toward the infield. Misiorowski's got a tight zone, and they'll be on alert for any hard-hit ball.

DeLuca takes a clean look at the four-seamer, 101 mph, swings and makes contact—called strike. Count now 0 and 1. Quiet as ever, just like he was in the opener. Misiorowski keeps the ball tight. Bases stay empty, top of the second moves on.

Slider 90 mph, just hangs there, touches the outside corner, called ball. Count now 1 and 1. DeLuca stays poised, just like in the opener. Misiorowski keeps the zone tight, ready for the next one. Bases stay empty, top of the second moves on.

Count sits at one and one now. Misiorowski deals another hundred and one mile an hour heater, DeLuca lifts it out to center, Mitchell drifts back and gathers it in for the second out, still brewers two, rays zero.
Misiorowski sets the stage, clean and steady, DeLuca ready to go. First pitch, no count, no runners, just the silence between breaths before the ball leaves the hand.

Victor Mesa Jr. takes a look at the four-seam fastball, 99 mph, swings and makes contact—called strike. Count now 0 and 1. Bases stay empty, top of the second moves on. Mesa’s got a sharp eye, new to the big leagues this season, but he’s steady in the clutch.

First game, and the Brewers lead 2 to 0, Mesa Jr. stepping in for the first time, with a .129 average in the post-season so far. Misiorowski’s 19 pitches keep things tight, and the series is still very much in the balance.
Count now 0 and 2. Mesa Jr. stays calm, just like in the opener. Misiorowski fires that 101 mph four-seamer, tight and clean, keeps the pressure on. Bases stay empty, top of the second moves on.
The Brewers got their runs early, two in the first, with Mesa Jr. making his debut, and now they’re holding on through the second, just like in the opening inning.
Victor Mesa Jr. strikes out swinging.

That takes care of the top of the second with zero runs and zero hits for Tampa Bay, leaving our Brewers ahead two to nothing. Let us pause for a quick word from our good friends at the ballpark before the bottom half gets underway.

Bob's Booth comes to you courtesy of Josh Stutting. Now, Josh may not play baseball, but folks, he knocks I T right out of the park. Tech trouble? Write to stutting dot josh at gmail dot com. That's s, t, u, t, t, i, n, g, dot, j, o, s, h, at gmail dot com.
Into the glove of the catcher settled the pitch, and Jacob Misiorowski is already up to twenty two pitches tonight as he handles the top of the second.

Nick Martinez deals to twenty two year old Cooper Pratt, zero and zero, and Pratt lifts a fly ball out to left field where Chandler Simpson settles under it for the first out, leaving our Brewers ahead two to nothing.
Ryan Braun was the National League Rookie of the Year in two thousand seven.

Into the glove of the catcher settled the pitch, a slider from Nick Martinez at 85 mph, called strike. Count now stands at zero balls and one strike. Sal Frelick, 26, from Boston, steps into the box, looking steady, with just one strike to go before the next pitch.

With the count 0 and 1, Martinez fires a sinker at 93 mph, ball, making it 1 and 1. Frelick takes the pitch, eyes steady, looking for a chance to get it over the plate. The ball sits down just outside the zone.

Martinez delivers a seventy eight mile an hour changeup, Frelick makes contact, sending a ground ball at eighty six miles an hour out toward right field. There it goes past the infield, a base hit for Sal Frelick, and our Brewers keep the line moving with one away in the second, still holding a two to nothing lead over Tampa Bay.

Hamilton drops down a bunt, Martinez fields it cleanly and throws to Williamson at second base for the out as Frelick moves up, two down now in the bottom of the second, and our Brewers still lead it two to nothing.
David Hamilton, 29, from San Marcos, steps up with a quiet calm—no hits yet tonight, but he’s been hot in the postseason, .455, 5 for 11, one HR. Just one swing to go.
Martinez winds up, fires a 94-mile-an-hour sinker, ball, count now stands at one ball and zero strikes. Chourio takes it, eyes on the plate, the ball just sitting there, a little off the edge.

Martinez fires a 94-mile-an-hour sinker, foul tip, count now stands at one ball and one strike. Chourio stays on the plate, eyes locked, the ball just brushing the outside corner. Two out, runners on second, Brewers lead two to nothing.
Chourio takes the pitch, Martinez fires a 79-mile-an-hour changeup, ball, count now 2 and 1. Runners on second, two out, Brewers hold a two to nothing lead.

The cutter slips just over the plate, a soft touch, lands in the dirt near the left side of the infield. Count now 3 and 1. Chourio stays on the plate, eyes locked, runners on second, two out, Brewers still lead two to nothing.
Martinez's in the box, Chourio at the plate, runners on second, two out—Martinez’s got that Tricky reputation, so watch for any sharp cut or late fade, especially to the outer part of the field.

Chourio swings at the 95-mile-an-hour sinker, makes contact, swings hard, it's a strike. Count now stands at three balls and two strikes. Runners on second, two out, Brewers still lead two to nothing.
The ball landed soft in the dirt near left field, just past the first-base line. First game, no wins yet—this one could be the one that changes everything.
Frelick sprints down to third, makes it safe. Count stands 3 balls, 2 strikes.

Martinez deals the ninety-five-mile-an-hour sinker, Chourio swings through it for the final strike, and that ends the inning Oh no, he got him with the sinker, I cannot believe it, just missed that one entirely, and the chance slips right away.

That half is over now. No runs on one hit for Milwaukee, leaving us two to nothing as the Brewers lead the Rays. Back before our boys took the field here, Milwaukee had the Braves, who won the nineteen fifty-seven World Series. Let us see what the third brings us.
A word from our sponsor, and frankly our only sponsor, Josh Stutting. When your computer throws you a curveball, Josh hits it into the upper deck. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
Bottom of the second now, three outs recorded with nobody on base, Milwaukee holding a two to nothing lead over Tampa Bay while Jackson Chourio steps in against Nick Martinez with zero and zero.

Ben Williamson comes up with the count at 1 ball, 0 strikes. Misiorowski fires a four-seam fastball, 99 mph, sharp and clean. The ball sits in the zone, Williamson watches it, takes a breath, and swings—no change in the count. One ball, nothing on the board.

Misiorowski fires a four-seam fastball, 101 mph, tight and crisp, Williamson watches it — one ball, one strike. The count settles at 1 and 1. Jacob’s got a fresh look tonight, 22 pitches so far, 8.1 innings in the postseason, 3.24 ERA.
With the count at 1 and 1, Misiorowski sends a four-seam fastball, 100 mph, sharp and clean. Williamson watches it, takes a breath, and swings—no change. Now it's 1 ball, 2 strikes.
Count's at 1 ball, 2 strikes, Williamson up against Misiorowski. A four-seam fastball, 103 mph, foul off the inside corner. Still 1 and 2.

Misiorowski slips a slider, 90 mph, just inside the zone. Williamson watches it, takes a breath—no change. The count goes to 2 balls, 2 strikes. Jacob’s been working the craft, keeps the ball in the pocket.
Count's at 2 and 2, Misiorowski slips a slider, 92 mph, ball. Now it's 3 balls, 2 strikes. Williamson stays back, eyes on the plate, the ball floats just outside, stays fair, no change in the count.

Misiorowski delivers the one hundred one-mile-an-hour fastball, Williamson hits a grounder toward first, Bauers takes it himself for the out, and that clears the base with one down in the third, Brewers still leading two to nothing.
Teddy Higuera won twenty games for the Brewers in nineteen eighty-six.

Misiorowski winds up, glove in his lap, hands steady, fires a four-seam fastball, 101 mph, clean and crisp, ball. Count's 1 and 0. Taylor Walls stands tall, eyes on the plate, just stepping into the zone.
Taylor Walls steps in, eyes on the plate. Misiorowski fires a four-seam fastball, 102 mph, clean and crisp, called strike. Count's now 1 ball, 1 strike. Jacob's keeping it tight in the pocket.

Jacob Misiorowski fires a curveball, 89 mph, just outside the zone. Taylor Walls watches it, takes a breath—no change. Count now 1 ball, 2 strikes. The pitcher's keeping it in the pocket, steady as ever.
Cutter 95 mph, foul, count stays 1 ball, 2 strikes. Walls keeps his eyes on the plate, stays ready. Misiorowski keeps the pace steady, no rush. One out, bases empty, Brewers up by two.
Taylor Walls, just turned thirty, came up in '21, and while he’s been around the majors, this postseason hasn’t seen much fire—only four hits in twenty-seven at-bats so far.
Slider 89 mph, foul, count now 1 ball, 2 strikes. Walls stays in the box, eyes locked. Misiorowski keeps the rhythm, calm as ever. One out, bases empty, Brewers up by two.
Misiorowski delivers a four-seam fastball, 101 mph, soft touch, ball. Count's now 2 balls, 2 strikes. Walls stays set, eyes on the plate. One out, bases empty, Brewers up by two.

Count’s now 2 and 3, Misiorowski fires a cutter, 94 mph, clean and sharp—called strike. Walls swings, feels the edge, keeps his head down. That’s it, two outs, bases empty, Brewers lead, 2 to 0. Oh, what a nice finish, steady as ever, just like the old days when I tried to catch fly balls in the dark.
Yandy Díaz sees a four-seam fastball, 102 mph, foul, count now 0 balls, 1 strike. Misiorowski keeps it tight, no hurry. Two out, bases empty, Brewers up by two. Díaz stays ready, eyes on the plate.
Slider ninety-three miles an hour, Díaz connects, sharp line drive at one hundred two miles an hour out to second, Turang squeezes it. That's three. Rays zero, Brewers two.

And that takes care of the top of the third inning. Tampa Bay goes quiet, no runs, no hits, leaving our score at two to zero in favor of Milwaukee. Let us stretch those legs while we get ready for the bottom half.
Got a computer that's been on the injured list all season? Josh Stutting is the trainer you need, and he'll have it back in the lineup by morning. stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
That brings up the next man. Age thirty-five and from Cuba, Díaz waits his turn.

Bottom of the third inning now, nobody out, bases empty, Milwaukee ahead by two runs to none. Nick Martinez looks in for his sign, delivers an eighty-five-mile-an-hour slider, and Jake Bauers fouls it away. That makes the count zero balls and one strike.

Four-seam fastball, 95 mph, ball, count now 1 and 1. Martinez, Tricky, keeps the zone tight. Bauers stays calm, eyes on the plate. The pitcher's got a long track tonight, 35 pitches already. One more to go, just keep it steady.

Changeup, smooth and slow, called strike, count now 1 and 2. Bauers stays patient, eyes locked on the plate. Martinez keeps the feel, working the zone. One more pitch to go before the count hits three.

Bauers takes a look at the four-seam fastball, 94 mph, lets it roll past the outside corner—ball, count now 2 and 2. Martinez keeps the zone tight, still in command. One more pitch to go before the count hits three.

Nick Martinez serves up an eighty-five-mile-an-hour slider, foul ball, count stays 2 balls and 2 strikes. Bauers watches the plate, stays cool, the pitch goes soft and wide, just beyond the outside corner.

Martinez deals the seventy-eight-mile-an-hour changeup, Bauers swings right through it for the third strike, and that's one away in the bottom of the third with the Brewers still holding a two-run lead.

Martinez’s been throwing hard all night, 41 pitches so far, keeping the count tight with a steady arm. His postseason strikeout total’s still just six, but he’s got that Tricky edge, working the zone like he’s been doing it since '14.
Sinker, 94 mph, called strike, count now 0 and 1. Yelich stays poised, eyes on the plate. Martinez keeps it tight, the first pitch of the at-bat. One out, bases empty, Brewers leading by two.

Slider, 85 mph, ball, count now 1 and 1. Yelich stays calm, eyes on the plate. Martinez keeps the zone, working the edges. One out, bases empty, Brewers leading by two. Yeli’s got a good feel, steady as ever in this postseason run.
Martinez delivers the seventy-eight-mile-an-hour changeup, missing just wide for a ball, count moves to two balls and one strike here in the bottom of the third with the Brewers ahead by two runs
Rollie Fingers won both the Cy Young Award and the MVP for the Brewers in nineteen eighty-one.

Martinez fires a 91-mile-an-hour cutter, Yelich swings and makes contact, the pitch is a swinging strike, count now 2 and 2. One out, bases empty, Brewers lead by two. Yelich stays cool, eyes locked on the plate.

Foul tip off the bat, count stays 2 and 2. Yelich stays ready, eyes on the plate. Martinez keeps the count even, the fourth-seamer hits the outer edge, just outside. One out, bases empty, Brewers leading by two.
Slider, eighty-five miles an hour, missing low for ball four, count is now full at three and two. Yelich takes his base quietly. One out, nobody on, Brewers still lead by two in the third.
Cutter, foul, count stays 3 and 2. Yelich stays poised, eyes on the plate. Martinez keeps the count tight, one out, bases empty, Brewers lead by two. The tension lingers, but the inning holds.

Misiorowski watches the corner, ready to step in if Yelich drives it deep. With Yelich on the plate and Martinez throwing from the back end, they’ll need sharp hands on the infield and eyes on the gap where the ball might hop.

Into the catcher's mitt that ninety-four-mile-an-hour four-seam fastball goes as Yelich swings and misses for the final out. Two down now in the third inning, and the Brewers still hold a two-to-zero lead over Tampa Bay.

Yelich steps up, clean slate, no balls no strikes, the first pitch of a game with no winners yet. Martinez’s first outing, the night’s first at-bat, and a quiet one, just waiting for something to happen.

Contreras takes the plate, count zero and one, foul tip off the bat. Martinez keeps it simple, one strike, no runners. The young catcher from Venezuela stands tall, eyes on the plate, ready for the next pitch.
Brewers got those two runs early, no pressure, just clean scoring. Contreras starts strong, first hit of the night, Martinez on the mound with a solid 49 pitches.

Martinez deals. Contreras lifts that sinker out toward right field where Victor Mesa Jr ranges over, settles underneath it, and makes the catch. That retires the side. Three down in the bottom of the third, score remains Brewers two, Rays zero.

That closes the third. Brewers still lead two to zero. Way back in nineteen eighty-two, Harvey Kuenn managed a group nicknamed Wallbangers that topped the big leagues in homers. Let us see what the top of the fourth brings.

This broadcast is brought to you by Brewers fans everywhere and by Josh Stutting, the man who taught a computer to call a ballgame. Technology needs, wizardry needs, whatever you've got: stutting dot josh at gmail dot com.
Game one of this autumn classic, folks, and neither side has a win to its name yet as we settle into the middle innings.
Aranda takes the plate, count one and zero, fast ball from Misiorowski, 101 mph, soft and clean. That's one ball, no strikes, the count moves to one and zero. Aranda stays calm, eyes on the plate.
Count’s 2 and 0, Aranda takes the plate, Misiorowski fires a four-seamer 101 mph, soft and clean. That’s one ball, the count moves to two and zero.

Aranda faces Misiorowski with the count at 2 and 0. A four-seam fastball, clean and sharp, gets called strike. The count moves to 2 and 1. The pitcher stays in rhythm, Aranda keeps his eyes locked on the plate.
Misiorowski fires a cutter, 97 mph, soft and clean. That’s a ball, the count moves to three and one. Aranda stays poised, eyes on the plate, the windup tight, glove low, bat ready.
Robin Yount is the Brewers' all-time leader in games played and hits.

Misiorowski delivers the one hundred one-mile-an-hour four-seamer, high and away, and that makes four, Aranda jogs on down to first base on the walk, nobody out now in the fourth, Brewers still leading two to nothing.
Next up on the mound, Misiorowski with 43 pitches on the board, and Aranda ready to take it deep at first. Just one more at-bat, and the Brewers might just keep that lead.

Chandler Simpson steps into the box, count at zero and zero. Misiorowski fires a four-seam fastball, 100 mph, sharp and clean—called strike. The count moves to zero and one. Simpson stays ready, eyes on the plate, the windup tight, glove low.

Simpson takes the pitch, Misiorowski fires a four-seam fastball, 101 mph, soft and clean—called a ball. The count is now 1 and 1. Runners stay on first, Brewers lead by two, still looking to keep the inning alive.
